title: DbContext in ASP.NET Core
summary: AddDbContext, the scoped lifetime, constructor options, and a minimal API backed by SQLite.

steps.title: Registering the context
body: In an ASP.NET Core app you do not `new` the context. You **register** it with dependency injection, and endpoints ask for it:
The context then takes its configuration through its **constructor** instead of `OnConfiguring`:
That is what makes the same context usable with SQLite in tests and SQL Server in production: the **app** decides the provider, not the context.

steps.title: Scoped: one context per request
body: `AddDbContext` registers the context as **scoped**: ASP.NET Core creates one per HTTP request, gives the same instance to everything in that request, and disposes it when the request ends.
That fits how a context works:
- It is **not thread-safe**. Two requests must never share one.
- It is meant to be **short-lived**: its change tracker grows with everything it has loaded. A context that lives for the whole app would hold every entity it ever saw.
- A unit of work maps naturally onto a request: load, change, `SaveChanges`, done.

So never register it as a singleton, never store it in a static field, and never inject it into a singleton service. For background work, create a scope (`app.Services.CreateScope()`) or use `IDbContextFactory<T>` (`AddDbContextFactory`) to make short-lived contexts on demand.

steps.prompt: A singleton `CacheWarmer` service takes `NotesDb` in its constructor. What goes wrong?
options: ASP.NET Core refuses (a singleton cannot depend on a scoped service), and if forced, one context would be shared by every request and thread
Nothing: the context is created once and reused safely
Each request gets a fresh context anyway
The context reconnects to the database on every call
steps.explain: In development, scope validation throws on start: *Cannot consume scoped service from singleton*. A context captured by a singleton lives forever and is used from many threads at once. Inject `IDbContextFactory<NotesDb>` instead and create a context per job.

steps.prompt: Match the registration to its lifetime or use.
pairs: Scoped, but instances are reset and reused for speed
Singleton factory that makes contexts on demand
Your own scope, e.g. to migrate at start-up
steps.explain: All of them give each unit of work its own context. Pooling saves the cost of building a context per request; the factory is for code outside a request.

steps.prompt: Arrange the start of `Program.cs` so the database exists before the app serves requests.
steps.explain: Services are registered before `Build`. After it, a scope gives you a context to create (or migrate) the database, and only then does `app.Run()` start serving.

steps.prompt: Complete a context that receives its options from dependency injection.
steps.explain: The constructor takes `DbContextOptions<NotesDb>` and passes it to the base `DbContext`. `Set<Note>()` returns the table.

steps.prompt: This program uses a context factory. What does it print?
code: using (var db = factory.CreateDbContext()) { db.Database.EnsureCreated(); db.Notes.Add(new Note { Text = "a" }); db.SaveChanges(); }
steps.explain: Each `CreateDbContext()` returns a new, independent context over the same database. Each counts the one note: 1 + 1.

steps.title: A notes API
prompt: Build a small web API backed by SQLite. **Run checks** starts your server and calls it.
- Register `NotesDb` with `AddDbContext` and `Data Source=notes.db`, and create the database at start-up (in a scope).
- `Note`: `int Id`, `string Text`. `NotesDb` takes `DbContextOptions<NotesDb>` in its constructor.
- `GET /notes`: all notes ordered by id (no tracking).
- `POST /notes` with `{ "text": "..." }`: save it, answer **201 Created** with the note (`Results.Created($"/notes/{note.Id}", note)`).
- `DELETE /notes/{id}`: 204, or 404 if there is no such note.
solution: await db.Notes.FindAsync(id) is { } note ? Results.Ok(note) : Results.NotFound());
template: public static async Task Run(HttpClient http)
var dojoA = await http.PostAsJsonAsync("/notes", new { text = "buy milk" });
Dojo.Eq("the first note gets id 1", "1", DojoWeb.Prop(await DojoWeb.Json(dojoA), "id"));
Dojo.Eq("GET /notes lists both, in order", "buy milk|call mum",
dojoList.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array ? string.Join("|", dojoList.EnumerateArray().Select(n => DojoWeb.Prop(n, "text"))) : "(not an array)");
Dojo.Eq("one note is left", 1, dojoAfter.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.Array ? dojoAfter.GetArrayLength() : -1);
hints: Endpoints take the context as a parameter: `(int id, NotesDb db) => ...`.
